entry.title: Nevis Laboratories: Columbia University's Sanctuary for Science

media:group.media:title: Nevis Laboratories: Columbia University's Sanctuary for Science
media:group.media:description:
Nevis Laboratories is a research facility operated by Columbia University's Physics Department. The Nevis campus houses the labs of a number of physics faculty members and one medical center research facility, and will soon welcome faculty from the School of Engineering. Around 70 faculty, postdocs, students, and staff are at Nevis at any given time during the academic year.
“Nevis has over 30,000 feet of lab space, as well as two large high-bay areas, which offers Columbia researchers a lot of flexibility with space that we can’t always get on the Morningside campus,” said John Parsons, a professor of physics and the facility’s deputy director. “It’s an exciting time to be at Nevis, which has been evolving to meet the demands of science since its inception.”
This video takes a look at Nevis’s current work, and its long history as a campus and a laboratory.

entry.title: Meet Dennis Mitchell, Dean of Columbia College of Dental Medicine

media:group.media:description:
Dennis Mitchell discussDennis Mitchell discusses what inspired him to become the dean of Columbia University College of Dental Medicine and how his career has prepared him for this role. entry.title: Columbia University Professor Michael Woodford Wins the 2026 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics

media:group.media:title: Columbia University Professor Michael Woodford Wins the 2026 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics
media:group.media:description:
On Monday, October 12, 2026, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026 to Michael Woodford, the John Bates Clark Professor of Political Economy at Columbia University, along with Robert E. Hall of Stanford for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization.
Woodford is the 16th Columbian to receive this prize in economics, and the University’s 89th Nobel laureate.
Woodford began his academic career at Columbia as an assistant professor in the Department of Economics in 1984. He held positions at the University of Chicago and Princeton University before returning to Columbia in 2004. He has been both a MacArthur Fellow and a Guggenheim Fellow. He is also an elected fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, as well as a fellow of the Econometric Society, of the Society for the Advancement of Economic Theory, and of the Society for Economic Measurement.
For more on Professor Woodford and his Nobel win, please visit Columbia News.

entry.title: A Celebration for Columbia University Professor and Nobel Prize Winner Michael Woodford

media:group.media:title: A Celebration for Columbia University Professor and Nobel Prize Winner Michael Woodford
media:group.media:description:
On Monday, October 12, President Jennifer L. Mnookin and the Columbia community toasted Michael Woodford, the John Bates Clark Professor of Political Economy and recipient of the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, in the Low Library Rotunda on Columbia University’s Morningside campus.
Surrounded by more than 100 family members, friends, students, University colleagues, and well-wishers, including fellow Nobel laureates Joseph Stiglitz and Martin Chalfie, Woodford, shared this year’s prize with Robert E. Hall of Stanford University for their work on the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization. His research has reshaped the theoretical foundations of stabilization policy, strengthening the tools policymakers use to respond to economic shocks.
“I appreciate that Columbia is the kind of place where we are allowed to try ambitious things,” Woodford said. “I think it is important to our society that there are at least a few institutions that believe that this is worthwhile. I’m very grateful to have had such a home.”
For more on Professor Woodford and his thoughts on winning his Nobel, please visit Columbia News.

entry.title: Understanding the Economic Dashboard of the 21st Century With Professor Joseph Stiglitz

media:group.media:title: Understanding the Economic Dashboard of the 21st Century With Professor Joseph Stiglitz
media:group.media:description:
Enjoy this clip from Trailblazers, a series of conversations with Columbia University faculty whose ideas shape our world.
Joseph E. Stiglitz is the co-founder and co-president of the Initiative for Policy Dialogue at Columbia and chief economist of the Roosevelt Institute. In 2001, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics for his analyses of markets with asymmetric information, and he was a lead author of the 1995 Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize. In 2011, Time named Stiglitz one of the 100 most influential people in the world. Stiglitz was a member of the Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) from 1993 to 1995, during the Clinton administration, and served as CEA chairman from 1995 to 1997. He was chief economist and senior vice president of the World Bank from 1997 to 2000.
Hear more episodes of Trailblazers by exploring Columbia's Impact at https://www.columbia.edu/content/explore-columbias-impact

entry.title: The Core Curriculum: The Heart of Columbia University’s Undergraduate Experience | Columbia Close-Up

media:group.media:title: The Core Curriculum: The Heart of Columbia University’s Undergraduate Experience | Columbia Close-Up
media:group.media:description:
“The object of education is to teach us to love what is beautiful.” – Plato, “Republic”
For more than 100 years, the Core Curriculum has been the defining element of a Columbia College education. This communal learning experience cultivates community-wide discourse and contemplation around seminal works, contemporary issues and humanity’s most enduring questions.
In this video, we speak with Larry Jackson, the Associate Dean of Academic Affairs and Director of the Center for the Core Curriculum​ at Columbia College. Professor Jackson explores the experience of reading the core curriculum and explains why Columbia continues to focus on an approach that has united the university’s undergraduates since the university’s founding.
For more on the program and to find a list of what the students are reading, please visit the Core Curriculum undergraduate admissions homepage.

entry.title: Remembering 9/11, 25 Years Later: Columbia Professor and Former FDNY Fire Chief Joseph Pfeifer

media:group.media:title: Remembering 9/11, 25 Years Later: Columbia Professor and Former FDNY Fire Chief Joseph Pfeifer
media:group.media:description:
Joseph Pfeifer stands in the 9/11 Memorial Plaza and describes how, on 9/11, he was 10 blocks north of the World Trade Center, and he looked up when he heard a plane. It was flying so low that he could see the word “American” on the fuselage. He saw the plane aim toward the North Tower. “It was no accident, but a direct hit.”
As the first battalion chief to report to the World Trade Center on that day, Pfeifer ordered firefighters to evacuate the people in the building. One of the firefighters he sent into the towers was his brother, Kevin, who died that day.
Since 2002, Pfeifer has been part of the Columbia University community. He teaches Principles of Crisis Leadership. What did it mean then, and what does it mean now? How do we use those principles?
“Leadership in a crisis,” says Pfeifer, “is not one person standing on a hill and giving orders. Leadership is bringing people together, collaborating, and then coordinating to deal with the problem at hand.” As he wrote in his memoir about 9/11, leadership is really about “Ordinary Heroes,” which is the title of his book.
The Columbia community, says Pfeifer, is part of his resilience, a place where he can share his message. “It’s where we can remember the people we lost on 9/11, and the people we saved. We also remember 9/12, when the world came together for New York City.”
To read more about Joseph Pfeifer and his teaching experience at Columbia, visit https://news.columbia.edu/news/what-911-hero-can-teach-columbia-sipa-students-about-crisis-leadership.

entry.title: A Snapshot of Summer With President Mnookin | Columbia University

media:group.media:title: A Snapshot of Summer With President Mnookin | Columbia University
media:group.media:description:
It has been a busy summer for Columbia University’s new president, Jennifer L. Mnookin. In this video, Columbia News provides a snapshot of just some of the many meetings and events she’s attended with faculty, students, staff, alumni, and our community, since officially taking the reins on July 1, 2026.
Featured clips in the video include: a faculty welcome breakfast; a Fourth of July picnic on Morningside campus for all staff; a visit with staff and students from University Life; a presidential staff meeting in Low Library; a summer celebration with Facilities and Operations; an employee appreciation ice cream social at the Medical Center campus; a School of General Studies summer event; a tour of the Law School, her new academic home, and the school’s new Li Lu Law Library; an outing at Butler Library to see some selections from the Rare Book and Manuscript Library; and a Community Partners breakfast with local elected officials, community leaders, neighbors, and University affiliates on the Manhattanville campus.
Watch this quick look back at summer as we get ready for the year ahead!
